rows: A waste exemption permits specified low-risk waste operations without a full environmental permit when all conditions are met.
Businesses should select the exemption that exactly matches the activity.
Waste types, quantities and operating limits must remain within the exemption.
Some exemptions require registration and may involve a charge.
Exemptions have location, duration and activity restrictions.
Multiple activities should be assessed separately.
Operations outside exemption conditions require an appropriate permit or cessation.
An exemption registration number does not prove that a particular waste activity complies.
Conclusions require exemption code, waste type, quantity, location, activity, dates, records and permit evidence.
Specified activities in or near main rivers, flood defences and sea defences may require an environmental permit.
Permit need depends on activity type and location.
Some activities may qualify for an exemption or standard rule.
Work should not begin until the required authorisation is in place.
Design should consider flood conveyance, defence integrity and environmental effects.
Landowner or other consents may also be required.
Permit conditions should be followed during and after work.
Changes to scope or location require reassessment.
Planning permission or landowner consent does not prove that flood-risk activity authorisation is complete.
Conclusions require exact location, main-river status, activity, dimensions, exemption, permit, method and condition-compliance evidence.
Discharges of pollutants to surface water or groundwater can require an environmental permit.
Permit need depends on the substance, source, destination and activity.
Some small or low-risk discharges may operate under general binding rules or exemptions.
Discharge routes and receptors should be accurately identified.
Treatment should be suitable for the effluent and receiving environment.
Monitoring and records may be required by permit conditions.
Pollution incidents should be stopped, contained and reported as appropriate.
Changes in flow, composition or discharge point require reassessment.
A drainage plan or treatment-unit specification does not prove that a discharge is authorised or compliant.
Conclusions require effluent source, composition, volume, route, receptor, treatment, permit, monitoring and incident evidence.
Farmers and land managers must take reasonable precautions to prevent diffuse agricultural pollution.
Nutrients should be planned and applied to meet soil and crop need.
Applications should take account of weather, soil and field conditions.
Manures and fertilisers should not be applied where there is a significant pollution risk.
Soil erosion and runoff should be prevented where reasonably practicable.
Livestock and vehicle management should reduce damage to soil and water.
Records should support nutrient and land-management decisions.
Pollution or repeated failures should trigger corrective action.
A nutrient plan or compliant application rate does not prove that a field operation presents no water-pollution risk.
Conclusions require field, soil, slope, weather, crop need, nutrient source, timing, buffers and runoff evidence.
